newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrican unions say bosses seek to retain apartheid.
newsitem.headline: SAfrican unions say bosses seek to retain apartheid.

text.p: South Africa's main labour federation vowed on Tuesday to win its battle with employers over workers' rights, saying the mining sector in particular refused to leave the apartheid era.
"While they profess to be for the new South Africa, they want apartheid legislation at the workplace," Congress of South African Trade Unions General-Secretary Sam Shilowa told a news conference.
"This we cannot allow. It would amount to the abdication of the struggle against apartheid oppression and exploitation."

Cosatu, which has nearly two million members, held a national one-day strike on June 2 in protest at positions taken by the employers' goruping Business South Africa (BSA), on proposed legislation setting basic conditions of employment.
Shilowa said Cosatu leaders would meet on June 24 and 25 to decide on further action to press their demands for more maternity leave, limited working hours and new rules governing Sunday work.
"We are going to emerge victorious. We are going to engage in action which will ensure they (employers) change their positions," Shilowa said, adding that a new strike was possible.

Business leaders have said strikes will harm the workers which Cosatu says it is trying to protect, by scaring off foreign investors and hobbling the government's ambitious plans for economic growth and job creation.
BSA failed to respond formally to a Cosatu deadline of June 16 for business to present new positions on their differences.
"We know that they do not support the need for change at the workplace and that they want apartheid to remain at the workplace," Shilowa said.
"We know they believe that we should work like slaves in the name of global competitiveness."
The labour leader said talks between Cosatu, business and the government on the issue should be called off and the proposed legislation be sent to parliament as quickly as possible.

Cosatu believed legislators of the ruling African National Congress, which is in a formal alliance with Cosatu, would ensure that the legislation was passed in a form favourable to workers, Shilowa said.
He said that mining giant Anglo American Corp, some of whose leading executives are in BSA, was the main stumbling block to agreement on working conditions.
